updates.text: When locating a target object, do not repeatedly cycle among the same few locations. After checking a location and observing that the target is absent, including after opening a container whose visible contents lack the target, prefer an unchecked admissible location over returning to a previously checked one. Use a deterministic forward sweep through location names/numbers or receptacle classes to compensate for limited history, and expand across genuinely different receptacle and surface types, including outlying or non-kitchen receptacles when present, before revisiting checked sites. At minimum, avoid choosing a location that appears in the immediately preceding observations/actions when another admissible unexamined location exists, unless a new observation indicates the target may now be there.

For clean-and-place tasks, follow dependency order: locate and acquire the requested target object; if its source container is closed, open it before taking the object; go to the appropriate cleaning fixture such as a sinkbasin when available and clean the held target; then go to the requested destination; if the destination container is closed, open it before placing; finally move or place the cleaned target into or onto the destination. Verify that the acquired object matches the requested target and do not substitute an unrelated object.

Only select actions that appear in the current admissible action list. If an intended location or action is absent, do not issue it and expect progress; instead choose an available alternative, such as another listed location or a currently available examine/open action, and continue the plan from there.

to.text: When locating a target object, do not repeatedly cycle among the same few locations. Use the current admissible location list, which enumerates all reachable receptacles, to plan the search: first check locations that plausibly hold the target type (for example the fridge or a countertop for food, a stoveburner for cookware, or a sinkbasin or bathtubbasin for a sponge or cloth), then move through other distinct receptacle classes, including outlying or non-kitchen ones such as a bathtubbasin, cart, or toilet when listed, before inspecting any location a second time. Do not spend many consecutive steps exhausting a single class such as all cabinets or all shelves; after a few instances of one class, switch to a different unchecked class. After checking a location and observing that the target is absent, prefer an unchecked admissible location over returning to a previously checked one, and avoid the location named in the immediately preceding observation or action when another unexamined admissible location exists, unless a new observation indicates the target may now be there.
